title: The one-person software business
question: Can a solo founder operate a useful software business with AI doing most of the implementation?
scope: A bounded public-source extension, not a rerun of the seed's fictional kiosk investigation, a company audit or a market experiment.

families.label: Copilot research
families.note: Two different study populations, with overlapping authors and GitHub/Microsoft interests. Not two fully independent vendor validations.

families.label: METR research program
families.note: The follow-up is from the same organization and includes returning participants. These are temporal updates, not independent replications.

families.label: SWE-bench authors
families.note: Academic benchmark construction and author-run evaluation, not a field trial or a business audit.

families.label: Google / DORA
families.note: Primary industry research summary from a cloud/AI vendor; observational responses and interviews.

families.label: Base44 transaction
families.note: Wix's disclosure and TechCrunch's reporting share founder/acquirer information. Independent newsroom does not make underlying financial claims independent.

families.label: Levels self-report
families.note: News18 attributes implementation to the game description and revenue to founder posts. The underlying posts and records were not independently inspected.

sources.label: S01
sources.title: The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot
sources.authors: Sida Peng, Eirini Kalliamvakou, Peter Cihon and Mert Demirer
sources.dateNote: First submission; inspected HTML v1. Experiment ran in May–June 2022.
sources.inspection: Primary paper: abstract, study design, timing/success definition and reported results; not a raw-data reanalysis.
sources.method: 95 professional programmers recruited through Upwork, randomly assigned to one JavaScript HTTP-server task with or without Copilot. Completion time ends at the first commit passing 12 provided tests.
sources.interest: Author affiliations include GitHub and Microsoft. It is vendor-connected primary research, not an independent business audit.
limitations: A single short task, early tool version and recruited freelancer population; no longitudinal maintenance, sales, retention or owner economics.
Passing the provided tests is narrower than real-world product usefulness or security.
The reported 55.8% faster task completion cannot be multiplied into company revenue or a universal productivity forecast.

sources.label: S02
sources.title: The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers
sources.authors: Zheyuan Cui, Mert Demirer, Sonia Jaffe, Leon Musolff, Sida Peng and Tobias Salz
sources.dateNote: Publication metadata uses June 1; page labels the preprint June 2025. Page metadata last modified August 19, 2025.
sources.inspection: Primary publication listing and abstract only; full-paper estimators, task definitions and replication data were not audited.
sources.method: Company-run randomized access experiments at Microsoft, Accenture and an anonymous Fortune 100 company. The abstract combines 4,867 developers and reports a 26.08% increase in completed tasks, standard error 10.3%.
sources.interest: Company experiments, Microsoft-hosted publication and overlap with the Copilot study authors. Larger field context is valuable, but not vendor-independent replication.
limitations: The abstract says individual experiments are noisy. Its pooled estimate is not a guaranteed gain for every developer.
Enterprise developers have organizational infrastructure and colleagues that a solo founder may lack.
Completed tasks are not revenue, durable code quality, AI's share of accepted implementation, or all-role founder time.

sources.label: S03
sources.title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
sources.dateNote: Historical February–June 2025 tool/task setting; the page now explicitly calls the result out of date.
sources.inspection: Primary methodological write-up, core result, generalization cautions, FAQ and current update notice; not a replication of the linked paper.
sources.method: 16 experienced contributors supplied 246 real issues in familiar large repositories. Issues were randomized to allow/disallow AI, primarily Cursor with Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet; recorded work and self-reported time were compared.
sources.interest: Nonprofit AI-evaluation organization, not a coding-tool sales report. Its funding and raw data were not independently audited here.
limitations: Small, selected, experienced contributor group and mature repositories; not representative of all software work.
Measures early-2025 tools, not the best available September-2026 workflow.
The authors explicitly reject the inference that AI cannot help other developers; their newer update must accompany this result.

sources.label: S04
sources.title: We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design
sources.dateNote: Follow-up began August 2025; describes late-2025 tools and early-2026 interpretation.
sources.inspection: Full methodological update including raw effect estimates, recruitment/task selection, reduced pay, concurrency and sample description.
sources.method: 57 developers, including 10 returning participants, across 143 repositories and over 800 tasks. Returning developers' time estimate is −18%, interval −38% to +9%; new participants' estimate also spans zero.
sources.interest: Same research organization and partly overlapping participants as S03. Not an independent corroborating vote.
limitations: Developers unwilling to forgo AI and AI-favored tasks were selected out; compensation fell from USD 150/hour to USD 50/hour.
Parallel agents complicate time measurement. The authors say their data is very weak evidence for the size of improvement.
This weakens a present-day blanket slowdown claim without establishing a precise current speedup, much less business viability.

sources.label: S05
sources.title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?
sources.authors: Carlos E. Jimenez, John Yang, Alexander Wettig, Shunyu Yao, Kexin Pei, Ofir Press and Karthik Narasimhan
sources.dateNote: Date of the inspected paper revision, arXiv:2310.06770v3. This is the original SWE-bench paper, not SWE-bench Verified or a current leaderboard.
sources.inspection: Primary paper task construction, reproducibility details and discussion of limitations. No benchmark code was downloaded or executed.
sources.method: Repository issue/patch tasks with execution-based tests; the paper releases 2,294 task instances. Its discussion notes the Python-only domain and limits of code testing alone.
sources.interest: Authors of the evaluation describe their own benchmark. A benchmark is not an independent audit of a deployed business.
limitations: Test-passing patches do not measure willingness to pay, retention, maintenance labor, support or profitability.
The paper itself cautions that execution-based testing alone is insufficient to guarantee reliable generated code.
No contemporary agent success-rate claim is made in this review, and no seed benchmark is substituted for a real run.

sources.label: S06
sources.title: Announcing the 2025 DORA Report
sources.dateNote: Dated primary announcement of the 2025 State of AI-assisted Software Development report.
sources.inspection: Official findings/method summary; full PDF, survey instruments and model estimates were not independently audited.
sources.method: Nearly 5,000 technology-professional survey responses and over 100 hours of qualitative material. The announcement reports positive relationships with throughput/product performance, but a negative relationship with delivery stability.
sources.interest: Primary industry research from Google, which sells cloud and AI products.
limitations: Observational relationships are not randomized causal effects.
Organizational and self-reported outcomes are not measured solo-founder profit or individual implementation attribution.
Positive throughput and negative stability can coexist; neither should be omitted to create a one-sided story.

sources.label: S07
sources.title: Wix Further Expands into Vibe Coding with Acquisition of Base44, a Hyper-Growth Startup that Simplifies Web and App Creation with AI
sources.inspection: Primary transaction terms and product description; no independent valuation, payroll or financial audit.
sources.method: Acquirer disclosure of approximately USD 80 million initial consideration plus performance-based earn-outs through 2029, with approximately USD 25 million employee-retention payments included in the initial consideration.
sources.interest: Interested acquirer promoting its purchase; forward-looking product language is not demonstrated operating performance.
limitations: Purchase consideration is not recurring customer revenue, profit or founder take-home.
A platform that generates users' software is not evidence that AI generated most of the platform's own accepted implementation.
Employee-retention terms contradict a zero-human-staff interpretation of the acquisition.

sources.label: S08
sources.title: 6-month-old, solo-owned vibe coder Base44 sells to Wix for $80M cash
sources.dateNote: Page metadata modified June 20, 2025; fetched version retained by response hash.
sources.inspection: Reported acquisition, attributed staffing confirmation and attributed founder profit statement. Linked founder posts were not inspected.
sources.method: Journalistic report: Wix confirmed eight employees. A May profit figure is explicitly attributed to the founder's X/LinkedIn posts.
sources.interest: Independent newsroom, but key staffing and financial inputs originate with Wix/the founder; same event family as S07.
limitations: The article does not present payroll records or an independent audit of receipts, costs, retained customers or AI's work share.
A founder-attributed USD 189,000 May profit figure is not verified six-month owner economics.
The correction to the solo narrative does not prove solo operation was impossible at an earlier, narrower stage.

sources.label: S09
sources.title: Man Builds $1-Million Business Using AI In Just 17 Days
sources.dateNote: Article shows first publication and update on March 19, 2025. Individual byline not preserved in the fetched extract.
sources.inspection: Public article successfully fetched. Underlying game execution, X posts, payments and staffing were not inspected. Direct snapshot request was blocked; the tool-returned excerpts are retained honestly without a raw-response hash.
sources.method: The article repeats the game's AI-made description and attributes USD 87,000 monthly recurring revenue to Pieter Levels' X posts. It annualizes a short launch-period claim.
sources.interest: Reported founder claims, not independent verification. This is the most directly AI-attributed commercial lead in this bounded corpus, but lower-grade evidence than the experiments.
limitations: No independently verified labor roster, weighted implementation ledger, complete costs, retention cohorts or six-month operating history.
Annualized run rate is not a year of realized revenue; the launch-period article does not establish persistence.
Neither the headline nor a reported AI-made label verifies the protocol's definition of useful solo operation.

claims.title: AI can shorten a bounded implementation task
claims.text: Peng et al. report 55.8% faster completion with Copilot in a controlled JavaScript HTTP-server task involving 95 recruited programmers.
claims.implication: A credible mechanism for implementation leverage exists; it is not merely a benchmark score.
claims.limit: One task with 12 provided tests does not measure running a business, maintaining a product or earning revenue.

citations.locator: Abstract; Study Design, recruitment and task-completion definition

claims.title: The supporting case extends into real workplaces
claims.text: Cui et al.'s primary abstract combines three randomized company experiments and 4,867 developers, reporting 26.08% more completed tasks (standard error 10.3%).
claims.implication: The positive case is not limited to one toy assignment: there is field-experimental evidence of useful implementation assistance.
claims.limit: This review inspected the abstract, not the full analysis. Enterprise task throughput is not solo-founder margin, AI-majority attribution or sustained operations.

citations.locator: Publication abstract: combined sample, estimate and heterogeneity

claims.title: Assistance has also increased implementation time
claims.text: METR's early-2025 randomized issue study found experienced contributors took 19% longer with AI. Its 2025 page now explicitly marks that result as out of date.
claims.implication: Model output can add review and integration work. A universal or timeless productivity promise is unsupported.
claims.limit: The 16-developer mature-repository setting is narrow. Do not present it as the current effect of late-2025/2026 tools; read the update beside it.

citations.locator: Methodology; Core Result; current update notice; generalization table

claims.title: Current speedup is uncertain—not a repeated slowdown
claims.text: METR's 2026 update reports a −18% time estimate for returning developers, with an interval from −38% to +9%. It warns that selection effects and parallel-agent timing make the size of improvement unreliable.
claims.implication: The strongest pessimistic result has aged. Improvements are plausible, but the new point estimate is not a precise present-day effect.
claims.limit: Same research program, partly overlapping participants, lower compensation, selected tasks and developers. Neither a clean independent replication nor proof of general speedup.

citations.locator: Raw results; selection discussion; Details of the productivity study

claims.title: Test-passing is not business viability
claims.text: Original SWE-bench evaluates repository issue patches through code tests, and its authors caution that execution-based testing alone cannot guarantee reliable generated code. No paying-demand or operating-margin outcome is measured.
claims.implication: Benchmark progress can support a capability mechanism, but it cannot directly establish this business claim.
claims.limit: This is a methodological boundary from the inspected original paper, not a claim about today's SWE-bench Verified scores or model rankings.

claims.title: More delivery can coexist with less stability
claims.text: DORA's official 2025 summary reports positive relationships between AI adoption and throughput/product performance, alongside a negative relationship with delivery stability.
claims.implication: Faster production can leave the sole operator with a downstream quality and operations burden.
claims.limit: The burden interpretation is an inference. DORA uses survey/interview evidence, not a randomized causal estimate or a solo-founder profit study.

citations.locator: Opening methods summary; AI, the great amplifier

claims.title: An AI app builder attracted a real buyer
claims.text: Wix disclosed approximately USD 80 million initial consideration for Base44, plus conditional earn-outs. Approximately USD 25 million of that initial consideration was allocated to employee-retention payments.
claims.implication: There is a concrete commercial signal for an AI software-creation product, stronger than an unverifiable demo alone.
claims.limit: An acquisition price is not recurring revenue or solo operation. The disclosure does not attribute most of Base44's own implementation to AI.

citations.locator: Acquisition announcement, transaction terms and team description

claims.title: Solo ownership is not solo operation
claims.text: TechCrunch reports that Wix confirmed Base44 had eight employees at acquisition; Wix's own release describes employee-retention payments.
claims.implication: This high-profile commercial example fails the protocol's one-operator gate at the reported acquisition stage.
claims.limit: The newsroom and release share acquirer information; they are not independent payroll audits. This does not rule out an earlier genuinely solo phase.

citations.locator: Paragraph beginning with the qualification that Shlomo was not truly solo

claims.title: Reported profit is not an audited operating record
claims.text: TechCrunch attributes a USD 189,000 May profit figure to Base44's founder posts. The article does not supply an independent six-month reconciliation of profit, labor, retention and AI-work share.
claims.implication: The story may point toward viable economics, but this review cannot upgrade an attributed monthly figure into verified sustainable owner income.
claims.limit: Underlying founder posts and accounting records were not inspected. The source's attribution is preserved, not treated as a false statement or independent proof.

citations.locator: Paragraph attributing profitability to Shlomo's X/LinkedIn posts

claims.title: A reported AI-made game reached reported revenue
claims.text: News18 repeats fly.pieter.com's AI-made description and attributes USD 87,000 monthly recurring revenue to Pieter Levels' posts. This is a suggestive implementation-to-commerce anecdote, not an audited result.
claims.implication: The positive case includes a reported product with commercial activity, not coding studies alone.
claims.limit: The article does not verify staffing, accepted AI-work share, costs, retained paying use or six months of operation. Multiplying monthly run rate by twelve does not create a year of receipts.

citations.locator: What Is The Game?; AI-Made Flight Simulator: A $1 Million Business; date line

claims.title: Implementation leverage is only one part of the business
claims.text: Positive task-time and throughput findings support a possible mechanism. The contradictory time result, uncertain update and stability relationship show why total founder labor and operations must be measured separately.
claims.implication: A narrow, low-stakes product with a technically capable human operator is a reasonable hypothesis to test—not a demonstrated general business model.
claims.limit: This is an analyst inference under the locked definitions. Different tasks, populations, dates and outcome units must not be pooled into one effect size.

claims.title: The end-to-end record bundle is still missing
claims.text: No source in this inspected corpus establishes all seven operating gates for one founder and product over the same six-month period.
claims.implication: The broad business claim is not established by this review. Absence in a bounded corpus does not prove impossibility or that no qualifying business exists.
claims.limit: This is a coverage judgment about nine inspected documents, not an exhaustive census of founders. Paying retention, complete costs, total time and accepted AI-work attribution remain unverified jointly.

citations.locator: Transaction terms, not a solo operating ledger
Attributed launch-period implementation and revenue claims

contradictions.title: Faster here; slower there
contradictions.analysis: A standard short assignment, enterprise task counts and familiar mature-repository issues have different requirements and denominators. The apparent tension is real; it is not a direct same-population numerical contradiction.
contradictions.resolutionObservation: Current-tool matched tasks with prespecified quality criteria and all human review/rework time would show where the gain actually transfers.

contradictions.title: A historical result is not a current constant
contradictions.analysis: METR explicitly warns that its earlier result is out of date. Its later point estimates suggest improvement, but selection and measurement problems prevent a clean effect-size update.
contradictions.resolutionObservation: A current prespecified experiment with credible recruitment, task-selection and concurrent-time accounting would materially change confidence in today's mechanism.

contradictions.title: Throughput and stability can move in opposite directions
contradictions.analysis: More completed work does not itself imply less maintenance or incident work. DORA's relationship is observational and does not negate the randomized throughput result.
contradictions.resolutionObservation: Measure accepted work, escaped defects, restoration time, support and all-role founder labor in the same longitudinal product.

contradictions.title: A solo-owner headline hides a team
contradictions.analysis: The acquisition can be commercially significant while failing the one-operator definition. Wix's employee-retention terms and attributed eight-person count are from the same transaction family.
contradictions.resolutionObservation: A dated, independently corroborated labor roster for a genuinely solo operating interval, not ownership alone, would resolve the gate.

contradictions.title: Run rate, profit and durable operation are different
contradictions.analysis: A launch-period annualized revenue claim and a founder-attributed profitable month can be true without proving six-month retained demand, full-cost owner income or sustainable workload.
contradictions.resolutionObservation: A same-period six-month reconciliation of receipts, refunds, costs, cohorts, all labor and accepted AI-work attribution would close the gap.

hypothesisAssessments.assessment: Implementation mechanism supported in bounded settings; end-to-end feasibility remains unverified.
hypothesisAssessments.limit: The same hypothesis can fit task gains without a viable solo business. No complete operating case was inspected.

hypothesisAssessments.assessment: Consistent with the measured outcome gaps and stability concern, but not directly tested with all-role founder time.
hypothesisAssessments.limit: Positive implementation and commercial signals prevent claiming bottlenecks always erase gains. Missing joint records do not themselves measure a bottleneck.

hypothesisAssessments.assessment: One prominent solo narrative has a definition problem; selection across all businesses and hidden labor in other stories are not measured.
hypothesisAssessments.limit: Randomized implementation gains challenge an all-hype account, not the specific business-selection mechanism. Attributed or unaudited claims are not evidence of dishonesty.

businessCases.label: Base44 at its reported acquisition stage
businessCases.note: Eight employees are reported; acquisition value and a founder-attributed profitable month do not supply the remaining joint operating records.

businessCases.label: fly.pieter.com as reported in March 2025
businessCases.note: The article supplies an AI-made attribution and a launch-period revenue claim, not an independent staffing, retained-use, work-attribution, cost or six-month audit.

gateAssessments.note: Base44 had reported employees. The flight-game report does not independently establish a complete labor roster.
No inspected evidence verifies the prespecified paying-customer floor and 90-day retention cohort.
An AI-made label or coding-tool access is not a prespecified weighted ledger of accepted work and rewrites.
Receipts, full costs and all-role labor are not jointly reconciled against the declared income/time floor.
Company age, a profitable month and annualized launch revenue do not establish six months satisfying all gates.
No business case supplies restoration, incidents and support records with sole human accountability.
No independent corroborator is shown inspecting a complete same-period record bundle.

verdict.headline: Conditionally plausible. Not established.
verdict.short: AI can help implement software. The leap to a useful, sustainable one-person business remains unverified here.
verdict.rationale: Positive experiments and attributed commercial activity support a mechanism; context-dependent productivity, operational tradeoffs and missing joint business records block a demonstrated existence verdict under the locked definitions.
verdict.recommendation: For a technically capable founder, investigate a narrow, low-stakes product with known customer needs and human ownership of acceptance, security and operations. Treat AI-majority implementation as a measured hypothesis. Do not infer demand from generated code or give unreviewed agents production authority.

strongestCases.label: The strongest supporting case
strongestCases.text: Randomized studies show implementation gains in specific settings, larger workplace experiments make pure toy-task dismissal inadequate, the newer METR update warns against a timeless slowdown claim, and reported AI-built products show a possible path to commerce. If a capable founder chooses a bounded product and keeps the saved time after review, the mechanism is credible. The crucial 'if' remains unmeasured end to end.

strongestCases.label: The strongest opposing case
strongestCases.text: Implementation acceleration need not lower total owner effort or create demand. Expert maintenance work has shown slowdowns; organizational evidence flags stability costs; a famous solo-owner example had employees; and reported revenue lacks the labor, cost and retention denominators needed for sustainable operation. These observations defeat a general proof claim, not every possible narrow success.

limitations: Bounded purposive review, not a systematic review or a census of viable businesses; absence of qualifying evidence is not proof of absence.
Research-date cutoff is September 19, 2026 UTC. Included studies cover older tools and specific populations; no claim of exhaustive coverage of the newest models.
Six provenance families are not six statistically independent replications. Several sources have vendor interests or shared underlying informants.
Cui's source is an abstract and DORA's source is an official summary, not an independently reproduced full-paper analysis.
Commercial figures are carefully attributed. No customer interviews, private accounts, payment records, source-code attribution audit, deployment or market trial occurred.
The customer, income, time and duration floors were chosen before collection to make this question falsifiable; other founders may rationally choose different floors.

Eight raw HTTP response hashes and nine local capture-file hashes are available; News18's successful fetch tool did not expose raw response bytes. Dynamic pages may change and full copyrighted pages are not archived.
Automated data/UI logic checks are not human review or a real-browser visual/a11y certification; the parent owns any browser review.
The 18 synthetic seed observations remain in a separate, MIT-attributed provenance baseline and never count as public evidence.
